title: It Was a Good Day / Isleys
hook: Good Day is really a 1977 Isley Brothers record
voiceover: Good Day is really a 1977 Isley Brothers record. Ice Cube's It Was a Good Day, 1992, from The Predator. DJ Pooh built it on Footsteps in the Dark, from the Isleys' Go for Your Guns album on T-Neck. What he changed: he took the intro groove, that guitar and the soft keyboard bed, and let it ride almost untouched under Cube. What makes it rap is the drums. Pooh put his own kick and snare over the loop so it sits at Cube's pace. The lesson is restraint. Sometimes the flip is knowing what not to touch. Save this, then go pull Go for Your Guns. Then tell me Thursday's flip.
caption: Ice Cube, It Was a Good Day (1992, Priority). Produced by DJ Pooh. Sample: The Isley Brothers, Footsteps in the Dark, Pts. 1 and 2, from Go for Your Guns (T-Neck, 1977). Pooh barely chopped it. The Isleys' groove runs under the whole record and the new drums do the heavy lifting. Restraint is a production decision too. What flip should I break down Thursday? Drop it below and I'll pick one.
cover_text: Good Day is an Isleys record

title: Blind Alley: Kane to Mariah
hook: One 1972 Emotions break runs from Kane to Mariah
voiceover: One 1972 Emotions break runs from Kane to Mariah. Blind Alley. The Emotions, from the album Untouched, Volt Records, 1972. Chicago sisters singing over a Memphis groove. The first bars are drums, bass and a guitar figure, and that's the break. 1988, Marley Marl loops it for Big Daddy Kane's Ain't No Half-Steppin'. The whole record lives on it. 1993, Mariah Carey's Dreamlover rides the same loop to number 1 on the Hot 100 for 8 weeks. Same 4 bars, a rap classic and a pop smash 5 years apart. I still cut it between 2 rap records because heads know it in 2 bars. Name a record on Blind Alley I missed. Best answer gets pinned.
caption: The Emotions, Blind Alley, from Untouched (Volt/Stax, 1972). The break: Big Daddy Kane, Ain't No Half-Steppin' (1988, prod. Marley Marl). Mariah Carey, Dreamlover (1993, 8 weeks at number 1). One Stax girl-group intro carried a Brooklyn rap classic and a pop record 5 years apart. That's the range of a good break. Which record on Blind Alley did I leave out? Best answer gets pinned.

title: When the rewind is earned
hook: Most DJs waste the rewind. Here's when it's earned.
voiceover: Most DJs waste the rewind. Here's when it's earned. A pull-up is a promise to the room that what just happened was special. Do it 3 times in a set and the promise means nothing. My rule: the room has to ask first. If the first 8 bars get a real reaction, hands up, someone shouting the words, I spin it back once, and I let the intro breathe before the drop. If nobody moved, no rewind, no matter how much I love the record. And never rewind out of a mix that went wrong. That's hiding a mistake behind a trick and everybody in the room hears it. What's your rewind rule? Drop it below.
caption: The rewind is currency. Spend it once a night and it buys you the room. Spend it every 10 minutes and it buys nothing. My rule is simple: the crowd has to react before I pull it back, and I never use it to cover a bad mix. DJs, what's your rule? Once a set, once an hour, never? Tell me in the comments.

title: Regulate / Michael McDonald
hook: Regulate is a 1982 Michael McDonald record underneath
voiceover: Regulate is a 1982 Michael McDonald record underneath. You asked for this one Monday, so here it is. Warren G and Nate Dogg, 1994, the Above the Rim soundtrack on Death Row. The whole bed is I Keep Forgettin', from McDonald's If That's What It Takes album, Warner Bros, 1982. Warren G kept the keys and the bassline almost whole and let them loop. What he changed was the drums, a heavier G-funk pocket, and the story on top, 2 friends and 1 bad night in Long Beach. That opening line, regulators mount up, is from the film Young Guns. It went to number 2 on the Hot 100. Save this, pull the McDonald original, then tell me what I break down next.
caption: You asked Monday, here it is. Warren G and Nate Dogg, Regulate (1994, Death Row, Above the Rim soundtrack). Sample: Michael McDonald, I Keep Forgettin' (Every Time You're Near), from If That's What It Takes (Warner Bros, 1982). The intro quote is from Young Guns (1988). Number 2 on the Hot 100. A soft-rock keyboard part became the most famous G-funk record ever made. Next Thursday's flip is yours to pick. Comments.
cover_text: Regulate is a Michael McDonald record

title: Ohio Players: Pleasure
hook: Own one Ohio Players record. Make it this one.
voiceover: Own one Ohio Players record. Make it this one. Pleasure, Westbound Records, 1972. Not the Mercury hits, the earlier Dayton stuff. The record you need it for is Funky Worm. Junie Morrison playing a squealing synth line over a slow funk pocket, and it went number 1 on the R&B chart in 1973. That squeal is the whole West Coast. NWA lifted it for Dopeman in 1987. Kris Kross rode it on Jump in 1992. Every G-funk whistle you've ever heard is a cousin of it. What to look for: the original Westbound pressing, part of the Pain, Pleasure, Ecstasy run with the same cover model. Send this to the one friend who still buys vinyl.
caption: Ohio Players, Pleasure (Westbound, 1972). The cut is Funky Worm, number 1 R&B in 1973, Junie Morrison on the synth. Sampled on N.W.A.'s Dopeman (1987) and Kris Kross's Jump (1992), and it's the blueprint for every G-funk lead you've ever heard. Look for the original Westbound pressing from the Pain / Pleasure / Ecstasy run. What's the record you'd never sell? Tell me below.

title: Sponsored (native test): trap = club tempo
hook: Trap and jersey club are the same tempo. Really.
voiceover: Trap and jersey club are the same tempo. Really. Paid partnership: [partner] sponsors this one and I'm using their software in it. Your library reads a trap record at 70 and a jersey club record at 140, so you think they can't mix. They can. 70 is half of 140. Same grid, one just feels half time. So I analyse everything into 1 tempo range, 70 to 140, and I tag the half-time records so they sit next to their doubles. Bring the club drums in on the 1, ride 8 bars, cut the trap hats. The room hears a gear change, not a tempo change. What's your go-to bridge from hip-hop into club? Drop the BPM.
caption: Paid partnership with [partner]. Ad. Their software is what I use to analyse the library in this reel, and the technique is mine. 70 BPM trap and 140 BPM jersey club sit on the same grid, one just feels half time. Tag your half-time records, keep them next to their doubles, and the bridge from rap into club is 8 bars. DJs, what's your hip-hop to club bridge? Drop the BPM below.

title: Dah Shinin' at 32
hook: 32 years ago this week, Dah Shinin' dropped
voiceover: 32 years ago this week, Dah Shinin' dropped. Smif-N-Wessun, Tek and Steele, January 10, 1995, on Wreck Records through Nervous. Every producer credit on that album is Da Beatminerz. Bucktown, Wrekonize, Sound Bwoy Bureill. Bucktown is the record I still reach for when a room needs Brooklyn. Here's the part nobody posts. Within a year the firearms company Smith and Wesson came after the name. So the follow-up came out under Cocoa Brovaz. Same 2 guys, same Beatminerz, a different name on the sleeve, because a gun company owned the words. They took the name back years later. Where were you when Bucktown was on every radio?
caption: Smif-N-Wessun, Dah Shinin' (Wreck/Nervous, January 10, 1995). Produced entirely by Da Beatminerz. The detail the anniversary posts skip: Smith and Wesson, the gun maker, forced the name change, so 1998's The Rude Awakening came out as Cocoa Brovaz. They went back to Smif-N-Wessun years later. Where were you when Bucktown dropped? Comments.

title: Planet Rock replayed Kraftwerk
hook: Planet Rock never sampled Kraftwerk. It replayed them.
voiceover: Planet Rock never sampled Kraftwerk. It replayed them. Afrika Bambaataa and the Soulsonic Force, Tommy Boy, 1982. Arthur Baker and John Robie in the studio. The melody is Trans-Europe Express, Kraftwerk, 1977. The rhythm idea is Numbers, from Computer World, 1981. But there's no sampler on this record. Robie played the melody line on a synth, and the drums are a Roland 808 programmed to feel like Numbers. That's what they changed: they moved a German electronic record onto a Bronx drum machine and made it hip-hop. Kraftwerk still got paid later, because a melody is a melody. Every electro, Miami bass and freestyle record after it owes this one. Save it, then tell me what I break down Thursday.
caption: Afrika Bambaataa and the Soulsonic Force, Planet Rock (Tommy Boy, 1982). Produced by Arthur Baker with John Robie. Source: Kraftwerk, Trans-Europe Express (1977) for the melody and Numbers (Computer World, 1981) for the rhythm. Nothing was sampled. The melody was replayed on synth and the drums are a Roland TR-808. Tommy Boy settled with Kraftwerk afterwards. Electro, Miami bass and freestyle all start here. What's Thursday's flip? Comments.

title: The Big Beat, Squier to Jay
hook: One 1980 rock drum intro is in 99 Problems
voiceover: One 1980 rock drum intro is in 99 Problems. The Big Beat. Billy Squier, The Tale of the Tape, Capitol Records, 1980. The first bars are huge dry drums and a hand clap. That's the break. 1985, Run-DMC cut it on Here We Go, the live Funhouse recording. 2003, Rick Rubin builds Jay-Z's 99 Problems on it, and the same year Dizzee Rascal drops Fix Up Look Sharp on it in London. 2012, Alicia Keys rides it on Girl on Fire. A rock drummer's intro, cut in the Bronx, then Marcy, then Bow, then pop radio. I still use it as a bridge from rap into club because those drums cut through anything. Name a record on The Big Beat I missed.
caption: Billy Squier, The Big Beat, from The Tale of the Tape (Capitol, 1980). The lineage: Run-DMC, Here We Go (Live at the Funhouse) (1985). Jay-Z, 99 Problems (2003, prod. Rick Rubin). Dizzee Rascal, Fix Up, Look Sharp (2003). Alicia Keys, Girl on Fire (2012). A rock record's 8-bar drum intro that never stopped working. Which record on The Big Beat did I miss? Comments, best one gets pinned.

title: Cuts beat blends on rap
hook: Long blends are killing your rap set. Cut instead.
voiceover: Long blends are killing your rap set. Cut instead. Heads grew up on radio mixes and mixtapes where the DJ cut on the 1 and the record just arrived. A 32-bar blend of 2 rap vocals is mud, 2 rappers talking over each other. What I actually do. For 90s and 00s rap, I quick-mix. Beat-match, cue the new record on the 1 of the verse or the hook, and slam the fader on the downbeat. 1 bar of overlap at most. Save the long blends for the instrumental sections, amapiano and club, where there are no words to fight. Rap wants punctuation, club wants a sentence. Which do you do, cuts or blends? Drop your style below.
caption: Rap records are vocal records. Two vocals over each other for 16 bars is not a blend, it's noise, and every head in the room hears it. Quick-mix on the 1, one bar of overlap at most, and let the record arrive. Save the long blends for amapiano and club, where the instrumental sections give you room. DJs, are you a cutter or a blender on rap? Tell me below.

title: Electric Relaxation / Mystic Brew
hook: Electric Relaxation is a 1972 Blue Note record underneath
voiceover: Electric Relaxation is a 1972 Blue Note record underneath. You asked Monday, here it is. A Tribe Called Quest, Midnight Marauders, 1993. The whole bed is Mystic Brew by Ronnie Foster, from Two Headed Freap, Blue Note, 1972. Foster was an organ player, and Mystic Brew is a slow soul-jazz groove, bass, keys and organ walking together. What Tribe changed: they took the opening bass and keys figure, looped it, and let it roll for the whole record with a harder kick under it. No chop tricks, just the right 2 bars. That's the Tribe way. Find the loop that already sounds like a song. Save this, go pull Two Headed Freap, then tell me the next flip.
caption: You asked Monday. A Tribe Called Quest, Electric Relaxation, from Midnight Marauders (Jive, 1993). Sample: Ronnie Foster, Mystic Brew, from Two Headed Freap (Blue Note, 1972). Tribe found 2 bars that were already a song and gave them drums. That's the whole philosophy of that group in one record. Go pull the Foster album, the rest of it is worth your time too. What should I break down next Thursday?
cover_text: Electric Relaxation is a Blue Note record

title: Kool and the Gang: Light of Worlds
hook: Not Celebration. This is the Kool and the Gang record.
voiceover: Not Celebration. This is the Kool and the Gang record. Light of Worlds, De-Lite Records, 1974. Before the pop hits, before the singer, when they were a Jersey City jazz-funk band. The record you need it for is Summer Madness. 4 minutes of Rhodes and a slow synth line rising, no vocal. DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince built Summertime on it in 1991, and that record won a Grammy. Countless mixtape intros since. How I use it: it's my cooldown record, the one I play under the mic at the end of a night. Look for the original De-Lite pressing. It goes for a bit more now, but it's still findable. Send this to the friend who thinks Kool and the Gang is wedding music.
caption: Kool and the Gang, Light of Worlds (De-Lite, 1974). Before JT Taylor, before Celebration, when they were a jazz-funk band out of Jersey City. Summer Madness is the cut: DJ Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince's Summertime (1991) is built on it and took home the Grammy. Original De-Lite pressing is the one to hunt. What's the record you'd never sell? Comments.
cover_text: The Kool and the Gang record

title: Sponsored (end-card test): last 3 records
hook: Most DJs end the set wrong. My last 3.
voiceover: Most DJs end the set wrong. My last 3. The last 15 minutes are what the room remembers and what the promoter books you on. DJs either peak too early and limp out, or play new stuff nobody knows. What I do. Record 1, the biggest sing-along in the bag, the one everybody has an opinion on. Record 2, the reset, 1 tempo down, so the room breathes and looks up. Record 3, the record that says goodnight, warm, slow, words people know, and I let it play to the end. No mix out. Lights up on the outro. Quick note: this reel is a paid partnership with [partner], details on the end card and in the caption. What's your closer? Drop it below.
caption: Paid partnership with [partner]. Ad. Sponsor details on the end card. The technique is the same one I use every weekend: the last 3 records decide whether you get booked again. Biggest sing-along, then a reset one tempo down, then the goodnight record played out to the end with no mix. DJs, what's the record you close on? Drop it in the comments.

title: Do You Want More at 32
hook: 32 years ago this week, Do You Want More dropped
voiceover: 32 years ago this week, Do You Want More dropped. The Roots, January 17, 1995, on DGC, Geffen. Black Thought, Malik B, Questlove on drums, Hub on bass, Rahzel on the beatbox. A rap album played live, no samples, in a year when everything else was loops. Proceed, Distortion to Static, Silent Treatment. Here's the part nobody posts. The keyboard player on that record is Scott Storch. Before he produced Still D.R.E., Candy Shop and Baby Boy, he was a Roots member playing Rhodes on a Philly rap record. The Roots don't get the sample credits, because there aren't any. That's the point. Where were you when Proceed dropped?
caption: The Roots, Do You Want More?!!!??! (DGC/Geffen, January 17, 1995). Black Thought, Malik B, Questlove, Hub, Rahzel, and on keys, Scott Storch, years before Still D.R.E. and Candy Shop. A live-played rap album in the middle of the loop era, and it still sounds like nothing else. Where were you when Proceed came on? Comments.

title: Big Energy / Genius of Love
hook: Big Energy is a 1981 Tom Tom Club record
voiceover: Big Energy is a 1981 Tom Tom Club record. Latto, 2021. The bed is Genius of Love, Tom Tom Club, Sire Records, 1981, the Talking Heads rhythm section, Tina Weymouth and Chris Frantz, on their own. That bouncy synth-bass and the guitar chirp. This is one of the most flipped grooves in rap history. Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five cut It's Nasty on it in 1982. Mariah Carey's Fantasy rode it to number 1 in 1995. Then Latto, 40 years after the original, and the remix brought Mariah herself back onto it in 2022. What changed each time is only the drums and the singer. The loop never needed help. Save this, go pull the original, then tell me what I break down Thursday.
caption: Latto, Big Energy (2021). Source: Tom Tom Club, Genius of Love (Sire, 1981), Tina Weymouth and Chris Frantz from Talking Heads. Same groove under Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five's It's Nasty (1982) and Mariah Carey's Fantasy (1995), and Mariah came back for the Big Energy remix in 2022. 40 years, one bassline, nobody has improved on it. Thursday's flip is your call. Comments.
cover_text: Big Energy is Tom Tom Club

title: Different Strokes, Syl Johnson
hook: Syl Johnson's 1967 grunt runs from PE to Wu
voiceover: Syl Johnson's 1967 grunt runs from PE to Wu. Different Strokes. Twinight Records, Chicago, 1967. 2 minutes of hard drums, a bassline that walks, a woman laughing, and Syl grunting on the beat. The drums and that grunt are the break. 1989, the Bomb Squad fold it into Public Enemy's Fight the Power. 1993, RZA runs it under Shame on a Nigga on Enter the Wu-Tang. 2011, Jay-Z and Kanye build The Joy on it, and Syl sued them over it, and they settled. He spent years chasing payment for that record. I cut this one into jersey club edits because that grunt lands anywhere. Name a record on Different Strokes I missed.
caption: Syl Johnson, Different Strokes (Twinight, 1967). One of the most sampled records in rap, and the man spent decades chasing the cheques. Public Enemy, Fight the Power (1989). Wu-Tang Clan, Shame on a Nigga (1993). Jay-Z and Kanye West, The Joy (2011), which ended in a lawsuit and a settlement. Which record on Different Strokes did I miss? Comments, best one gets pinned.

title: When to touch the mic
hook: You don't need to talk on the mic. Mostly.
voiceover: You don't need to talk on the mic. Mostly. Most DJs grab the mic when they're nervous, and the room feels it. What I actually do. 3 moments, that's it. The first record: a name and a thank you, 5 words, then out. The reset: when I drop a tempo on purpose, 1 line so the room knows it's a choice, not a mistake. The end: the goodnight, the next DJ's name, and the promoter's name. Everything else, the record does the talking. If you feel the urge to hype a drop, cut the low end for 2 bars instead. The room reacts harder to silence than to shouting. Do you talk on the mic? Tell me when.
caption: Three mic moments a night: the hello, the reset, the goodnight. Everything else the records can say better than I can. The urge to hype a drop is really the urge to be seen, and a 2-bar low-end cut gets a bigger reaction than any shout. DJs, do you talk on the mic, and when? Tell me below.

title: Int'l Players Anthem / Willie Hutch
hook: Int'l Players Anthem is a 1973 Willie Hutch record
voiceover: Int'l Players Anthem is a 1973 Willie Hutch record. You asked Monday. UGK featuring OutKast, 2007, from Underground Kingz. Produced by DJ Paul and Juicy J of Three 6 Mafia. The bed is I Choose You, Willie Hutch, from The Mack soundtrack on Motown, 1973. A wedding song from a pimp film. What they changed is the shape. Andre 3000 raps his whole opening verse over the sample with no drums at all, just Hutch's strings and choir under him. Then the drums drop for Pimp C. The restraint is the flip. Everyone knows the wedding video. Fewer people have sat with the Hutch record, and it's Houston and Atlanta waiting to happen. Save this, pull The Mack, tell me the next one.
caption: You asked Monday. UGK feat. OutKast, Int'l Players Anthem (I Choose You) (Jive, 2007). Produced by DJ Paul and Juicy J. Sample: Willie Hutch, I Choose You, from The Mack soundtrack (Motown, 1973). Andre's first verse has no drums. That decision is the record. Port Arthur, Atlanta, Memphis and Motown on one song. Which flip do I break down next Thursday?

title: Donald Byrd: Stepping into Tomorrow
hook: The Donald Byrd record jazz snobs skip. DJs don't.
voiceover: The Donald Byrd record jazz snobs skip. DJs don't. Stepping into Tomorrow, Blue Note, 1975. Produced by the Mizell brothers, Larry and Fonce, in their Sky High run. The purists hated this era, a hard bop trumpet player making smooth, layered funk with vocals. The purists were wrong. The record you need it for is Think Twice. Slow, warm, a bassline you already know. Main Source built Looking at the Front Door on it in 1990, a breakup rap that still hurts. Erykah Badu covered it years later. How I use it: an early-night record, when the room is filling and I want heads nodding before they dance. Look for the original Blue Note pressing, blue and white label. What's the record you'd never sell?
caption: Donald Byrd, Stepping into Tomorrow (Blue Note, 1975), produced by Larry and Fonce Mizell. The jazz critics hated the Mizell era. The DJs never did. Think Twice is under Main Source's Looking at the Front Door (1990), and Erykah Badu covered it outright. Original 70s Blue Note pressing, blue and white label, is the one to look for. What's the record you'd never sell? Comments.
cover_text: The Donald Byrd record DJs keep

title: Sponsored (native test): ears are the gear
hook: Your ears are the only gear you can't replace
voiceover: Your ears are the only gear you can't replace. Paid partnership: [partner] make the earplugs I'm wearing in this one, and I'd say this either way. Club booths run loud for hours, and the ringing you get at 2am doesn't always leave. What I actually do. Filtered musician plugs in from soundcheck, not just at the peak. They take the level down without turning the mix to mud, so I can still hear the kick against the log drum. Booth monitor as low as I can mix on. Headphones only for the cue, 1 ear, then off. And 1 quiet hour after every gig before I put anything else in my ears. What do you do to protect yours? Serious question.
caption: Paid partnership with [partner]. Ad. These are the filtered plugs I'm wearing in the reel, and the habits are ones I'd tell you about with or without a sponsor. Plugs in from soundcheck, booth monitor low, one-ear cueing, and an hour of quiet after every gig. Tinnitus ends careers quietly. DJs, what do you do to protect your ears? Tell me in the comments, I read all of them.

title: The Documentary at 22
hook: 22 years ago this week, The Documentary dropped
voiceover: 22 years ago this week, The Documentary dropped. The Game, January 18, 2005, Aftermath, G-Unit and Interscope. Dr. Dre and 50 Cent behind him, Compton on the cover. It sold about 586,000 copies in its first week and debuted at number 1. How We Do, Dreams, Hate It or Love It. Here's the part nobody posts. Hate It or Love It wasn't a Dre beat. Cool and Dre, out of Miami, built it on Rubber Band by The Trammps, a 1975 Philly soul record, and it went to number 2 on the Hot 100. A West Coast comeback album, a Miami production team, a Philadelphia sample. That's how rap works. Where were you when How We Do came on?
caption: The Game, The Documentary (Aftermath/G-Unit/Interscope, January 18, 2005). About 586,000 first week, number 1 debut. The detail that gets skipped: Hate It or Love It is a Cool and Dre production out of Miami, built on The Trammps' Rubber Band (1975), and it peaked at number 2. Compton album, Miami beat, Philly sample. Where were you when How We Do dropped? Comments.

title: Ready or Not / Enya
hook: Ready or Not is really an Enya record
voiceover: Ready or Not is really an Enya record. The Fugees, The Score, 1996. The whole eerie bed is Boadicea, Enya, 1987, from her first album on BBC Records, and the hook is a rewrite of the Delfonics' Ready or Not Here I Come, Philly Groove, 1968, a Thom Bell production. What they changed: they looped the Enya choir, put a slow hip-hop kick and snare under it, and had Lauryn sing the Delfonics line on top. Here's the story. Nobody asked Enya. She found out after it was a hit, considered suing, and settled for a credit instead. Everyone assumed it was a soul sample. It's an Irish new-age record from 1987. Save this and tell me what I break down Thursday.
caption: Fugees, Ready or Not (Ruffhouse/Columbia, 1996). Sources: Enya, Boadicea (BBC Records, 1987), uncleared at first, settled with a credit after Enya found out. Hook: The Delfonics, Ready or Not Here I Come (Can't Hide from Love) (Philly Groove, 1968, prod. Thom Bell). A new-age choir and a Philly soul hook became the darkest record on The Score. What flip should I break down Thursday? Comments.

title: Mardi Gras bells, Bob James
hook: Those bells in Peter Piper are Bob James, 1975
voiceover: Those bells in Peter Piper are Bob James, 1975. Take Me to the Mardi Gras, from the album Two, on CTI. It's a Paul Simon song. Bob James covered it as a jazz-funk instrumental, and the first 8 bars are drums and those bells, no bass. That's the break. 1983, the Crash Crew cut Breaking Bells on it. 1986, Run-DMC's Peter Piper, the whole record, and the Beastie Boys' Hold It Now Hit It the same year. 2002, Missy's Work It samples Peter Piper, so the bells ride again through a Timbaland record. Paul Simon to Bob James to Queens to Virginia. I still cut those bells into jersey club at 140 and the room knows. Name a record on Mardi Gras I missed.
caption: Bob James, Take Me to the Mardi Gras, from Two (CTI, 1975). A Paul Simon cover. The bells: Crash Crew, Breaking Bells (1983). Run-DMC, Peter Piper (1986). Beastie Boys, Hold It Now, Hit It (1986). Missy Elliott, Work It (2002), by way of Peter Piper. Eight bars of bells and drums that Queens turned into a language. Which record on Mardi Gras did I leave out? Best answer gets pinned.

title: The handover
hook: Playing after another DJ is a skill. Here's mine.
voiceover: Playing after another DJ is a skill. Here's mine. The handover is where most nights get clumsy. The room drops, the tempo lurches, someone's USB is still in the deck. What I actually do. I'm in the booth 15 minutes early, headphones on, listening to what they're playing, not talking. I ask 1 question: what's your last record. Then I pick my first from their last, same tempo, same feel, so the room never hears a seam. First 2 records, I'm still in their set. Record 3 is where I turn the wheel. And I never cut their closer short. Let it finish. It's their night until the fader says it isn't. How do you handle handovers? Tell me below.
caption: The handover is the most under-practised 5 minutes in DJing. In the booth early, listen, ask what their last record is, and build your first two from it so the room never hears the seam. Turn the wheel on record 3, not record 1. And never cut another DJ's closer. DJs, what's your handover rule? Comments.

title: The Light / Bobby Caldwell
hook: The Light is a 1980 Bobby Caldwell record underneath
voiceover: The Light is a 1980 Bobby Caldwell record underneath. You asked Monday, here it is. Common, Like Water for Chocolate, 2000. Produced by J Dilla. The bed is Open Your Eyes, Bobby Caldwell, from the Cat in the Hat album, 1980. A Miami soul singer most people only know for What You Won't Do for Love. What Dilla changed: he took the opening chords and Caldwell's voice, let the sample swing a little loose against a tight kick, and cut it so the words land as a hook. Dilla's whole feel, in 1 loop. It was nominated for a Grammy for Best Rap Solo Performance. One of the great rap love songs, built on a smooth soul record nobody was digging for. Save this and tell me the next flip.
caption: You asked Monday. Common, The Light, from Like Water for Chocolate (MCA, 2000). Produced by J Dilla. Sample: Bobby Caldwell, Open Your Eyes, from Cat in the Hat (Clouds, 1980). Grammy nominated for Best Rap Solo Performance. Dilla let the loop breathe slightly out of step with the drums, and that looseness is the whole feel of the record. Next Thursday's flip is yours to pick.

title: Marvin Gaye: I Want You
hook: The Marvin Gaye record that's also a painting
voiceover: The Marvin Gaye record that's also a painting. I Want You, Tamla, 1976. Written and produced with Leon Ware, who had most of it built as his own album before Marvin heard it and took it. Slow, humid, whispered, and DJs play it as a set-closer for a reason. The cover is The Sugar Shack, a painting by Ernie Barnes, the same one in the end credits of Good Times. Look at it once and you'll recognise it the rest of your life. Camp Lo recreated it for Uptown Saturday Night, and we'll get to that on Sunday. Look for the original Tamla pressing. If it's clean, don't think twice. Send this to the one friend who still buys vinyl.
caption: Marvin Gaye, I Want You (Tamla, 1976). Co-written and produced with Leon Ware. The cover is Ernie Barnes' The Sugar Shack, the painting from the Good Times end credits, with the album title added for Marvin. Camp Lo rebuilt that cover for Uptown Saturday Night, which turns 30 on Sunday. A record you can hang on a wall. What's the record you'd never sell? Comments.

title: Sponsored (end-card test): USB backup
hook: A dead USB ends your set. Mine can't.
voiceover: A dead USB ends your set. Mine can't. Every DJ has the moment: the deck says no drive, the record is 40 seconds from ending, and the room is looking at you. What I actually do. 2 sticks, identical, exported from the same library the same night, 1 in each deck, so a dead port and a dead stick are both covered. A third in my jacket with just the Saturday bag on it. Phone with those same 30 records as files and a cable that fits the mixer, in case both decks go. And I test every stick in the booth before the first record, not after. This reel is a paid partnership with [partner], details on the end card and in the caption. What's your backup?
caption: Paid partnership with [partner]. Ad. Sponsor details on the end card. The backup plan is mine and it's saved more than one night: two identical sticks exported the same night, one in each deck, a third in my pocket with the 30-record bag, and the phone as a last resort. Test every stick before the first record. DJs, what's your backup when the deck says no drive? Comments.
cover_text: A dead USB can't end mine

title: Uptown Saturday Night at 30
hook: 30 years ago this week, Uptown Saturday Night dropped
voiceover: 30 years ago this week, Uptown Saturday Night dropped. Camp Lo, Geechi Suede and Sonny Cheeba, January 28, 1997, on Profile Records. Ski Beatz produced almost all of it, right after Reasonable Doubt. Luchini, Coolie High, Black Nostaljack. 2 kids from the Bronx rapping like it was 1974 in slang nobody could fully decode, over Ski's loops. Here's the part nobody posts. Luchini is built on Adventures in the Land of Music by Dynasty, a 1980 Solar Records boogie group. And the cover is Ernie Barnes' Sugar Shack redone with Camp Lo in the room, the Marvin Gaye I Want You cover, on purpose. The whole album is a 70s film they wrote themselves. Where were you when Luchini came on?
caption: Camp Lo, Uptown Saturday Night (Profile, January 28, 1997). Produced mostly by Ski Beatz straight off Reasonable Doubt. Luchini (AKA This Is It) rides Dynasty's Adventures in the Land of Music (Solar, 1980). The cover recreates Ernie Barnes' Sugar Shack from Marvin Gaye's I Want You, the record we covered Friday. 30 years and nobody has made anything that sounds like it. Where were you when Luchini dropped?

title: Money Trees / Beach House
hook: Money Trees is a Beach House record played backwards
voiceover: Money Trees is a Beach House record played backwards. Kendrick Lamar, good kid, m.A.A.d city, 2012, Jay Rock on the last verse. Produced by DJ Dahi. The bed is Silver Soul, Beach House, from Teen Dream on Sub Pop, 2010. An indie dream-pop record from Baltimore, 2 years old when Dahi found it. What he changed: he reversed the guitar and vocal so the melody swims backwards, looped it, and put a slow Compton knock under it. The reverse is why it feels like a memory instead of a song. Everybody hears the chorus. Almost nobody has heard the original going forwards. Save this, go pull Teen Dream, then tell me what I break down Thursday.
caption: Kendrick Lamar feat. Jay Rock, Money Trees (TDE/Aftermath/Interscope, 2012). Produced by DJ Dahi. Sample: Beach House, Silver Soul, from Teen Dream (Sub Pop, 2010), reversed. A Baltimore dream-pop record two years old at the time became one of the most played Kendrick songs ever. Sample sources don't have to be old. They have to be right. What flip do I break down Thursday? Comments.
cover_text: Money Trees is Beach House backwards

title: Scorpio, Dennis Coffey
hook: Scorpio went top 10 in 1972. Then rap took it.
voiceover: Scorpio went top 10 in 1972. Then rap took it. Dennis Coffey and the Detroit Guitar Band, Sussex Records, 1971, from the album Evolution. Coffey was a Funk Brother, the Motown session guitarist on Cloud Nine and Psychedelic Shack. Scorpio is 4 minutes of congas, a fat bassline and a drum break in the middle, and it went to number 6 on the Hot 100. He played it on Soul Train. Then the Bronx got hold of the break. 1989, Young MC's Know How rides it, and LL Cool J's Jingling Baby the same year. I still cut it when a room needs a lift without changing tempo. Name a record on Scorpio I missed.
caption: Dennis Coffey and the Detroit Guitar Band, Scorpio, from Evolution (Sussex, 1971). Number 6 on the Hot 100 in 1972, played on Soul Train by a Motown Funk Brother. The break lives on Young MC's Know How (1989) and LL Cool J's Jingling Baby (1989), and it's a park-jam staple long before either. Which record on Scorpio did I miss? Comments, best answer gets pinned.
